Run all of these commands in your terminal,
from inside your project folder (except `git clone`, which creates the folder for you).
For the full explanations, see the textbook chapters on
[Git basics](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/git-basics.html),
[Git history](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/git-history.html),
[Git branches](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/git-branches.html), and
[merge conflicts](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/git-merge-conflicts.html).

---

## 📍 The Everyday Workflow

| Task | Command |
|------|---------|
| Clone a remote version control repository from GitHub.com to your local computer | `git clone <URL>` |
| Check the status of the local version control repository | `git status` |
| Add a file to the staging area | `git add <FILENAME>` |
| Commit staged files to the version control history | `git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes"` |
| Push changes from the local repository to the remote repository on GitHub.com | `git push` |
| Pull changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com to the local repository | `git pull` |
| View the version control history | `git log` |

The usual loop is: `git pull` → edit files → `git status` → `git add` → `git commit` → `git push`.

---

## 📍 Getting a Repository

1. `git clone <URL>` — Copy a remote repository from GitHub.com to your computer  
    - Example: `git clone https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students.git`  
    - This creates a new folder named after the repository.
      Use `cd <folder_name>` to go into it.  
    - Do not clone a repository inside another repository.
2. `git init` — Turn the current folder into a new, empty Git repository  
    - Only needed when you start a project locally.
      If you start on GitHub.com and then `git clone`, you do not need it.

---

## 📍 Checking the Status

3. `git status` — Show which files are modified, staged, or not tracked yet  
    - Run it often, especially before `git add` and `git commit`.
4. `git diff` — Show the changes you made that are not staged yet  
    - `git diff --staged` — Show the changes that are staged and will go into the next commit

---

## 📍 Staging and Committing

5. `git add <FILENAME>` — Add a file to the staging area  
    - `git add <FILE1> <FILE2>` — Add several files at once  
    - `git add <FOLDER>/` — Add everything in a folder  
    - `git add .` — Add all changes in the current folder (check `git status` first so you only stage what you mean to)
6. `git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes"` — Commit the staged files to the version control history  
    - Write a short, specific message that says what changed and why.
    - Only staged files are committed.
7. `git restore --staged <FILENAME>` — Unstage a file (your edits to the file are kept)
8. `git restore <FILENAME>` — Discard your unstaged edits to a file and go back to the last commit  
    - ⚠️ This cannot be undone.

---

## 📍 Syncing with GitHub

9. `git push` — Send your local commits to the remote repository on GitHub.com  
    - First push of a new branch: `git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME>` (`-u` stands for `--set-upstream`).
      See the branches section below for the difference between this and `git push origin <BRANCH_NAME>`.
10. `git pull` — Get changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com
    and merge them into your local repository  
    - Pull before you start working, and before you push, to avoid conflicts.
11. `git fetch` — Download the latest changes from GitHub.com without merging them into your files
12. `git remote -v` — Show the URL of the remote repository your local repository is connected to

---

## 📍 Viewing the History

13. `git log` — View the version control history  
    - Press `q` to exit the log.
      Use the arrow keys, `b`, or the space bar to scroll.  
    - Press `/` + a search term + `Enter` to search the log; `n` / `N` jump to the next / previous match.  
    - `git log -n 3` — Show only the last 3 commits  
    - `git log <FILENAME>` — Show only the commits that changed this file
14. `git show <COMMIT_ID>` — Show the changes made in one commit  
    - The commit ID (also called the commit hash, or SHA) is the long string of letters
      and numbers after `commit` in `git log`.
      It is a hash of the commit's contents, so each commit has a unique one.  
    - The first 7 characters (the short SHA) are usually enough: `git show 238dbcb`

::: callout-tip
## 💡 Just want a look at the past?

On GitHub.com, click the **commits** link on the repository's main page to see the history and commit messages.
Click the **<>** button next to a commit to view the state of the whole repository at that point in time.
:::

---

## 📍 Going Back in Time

Use these in your local repository when you want to run or explore files from the past,
or bring a past version of a file into the present.

15. `git checkout <COMMIT_ID> .` — Move the whole project (all files and directories) back to the state of that commit  
    - The last `.` is really important, so don't forget it!  
    - Example: `git checkout 9b4af1d .`  
    - The files now look like they did at that commit, so you can explore and run them.
16. `git checkout HEAD .` — Go back to the future: return to the most recent commit  
    - `HEAD` is the nickname for the most recent commit.  
    - Run `git log` afterwards to check you returned safely.
17. `git checkout <COMMIT_ID> <FILENAME>` — Bring back the version of a single file from a past commit  
    - Example: `git checkout 5837143 doc/count_report.Rmd`  

---

## 📍 Branches

18. `git branch` — List the local branches (the current one is marked with `*`)  
    - `git branch -v` — Also show the SHA
      and message of the last commit on each branch (`-v` stands for `--verbose`)
    - `git branch -a` — Also list the branches on the remote
19. `git switch -c <BRANCH_NAME>` — Create a new branch and switch to it  
    - Same as `git checkout -b <BRANCH_NAME>`  
    - Use a descriptive name, e.g. `patch-docs` for a fix to the documentation.
20. `git switch <BRANCH_NAME>` — Switch to an existing branch (no `-c`, since we are not creating one)  
    - Same as `git checkout <BRANCH_NAME>`
21. `git fetch --all` — Download all changes to all branches from the remote,
    so you can switch to a branch a collaborator created
22. `git push origin <BRANCH_NAME>` — Push the changes on a branch to the remote repository (usually named `origin`)  
    - This pushes once.
      Git does not remember the connection,
      so a plain `git push` on that branch fails with `fatal: The current branch <BRANCH_NAME> has no upstream branch`,
      and you have to type `git push origin <BRANCH_NAME>` every time.  
    - `git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME>` — Push *and* link your local branch to the remote branch of the same name (`-u` stands for `--set-upstream`).
      After this, plain `git push` and `git pull` work on that branch,
      and `git status` tells you whether you are ahead of or behind the remote.  
    - You only need `-u` the first time you push a new branch.
23. `git merge <BRANCH_NAME>` — Merge the branch `<BRANCH_NAME>` into the branch you are currently on  
    - If the same lines were changed in both branches, Git stops with a **merge conflict**.
      Open the files with `<<<<<<<` markers, choose what to keep, then `git add` and `git commit`.
25. `git branch -d <BRANCH_NAME>` — Delete a local branch that has been merged


::: callout-tip
## 💡 Typical branch workflow

1. `git switch main` and `git pull` — start from the latest `main`
2. `git switch -c my-new-feature` — create a branch
3. Edit, `git add`, `git commit` (repeat as needed)
4. `git push -u origin my-new-feature` — push the branch
5. Open a pull request on GitHub.com, get it reviewed, and merge it there
6. `git switch main` and `git pull` — bring the merged work back to your computer
:::

---

## 📍 Ignoring Files

`.gitignore` — A text file in the root of the repository listing files
and folders that Git should not track  
    - One pattern per line, e.g. `.venv/`, `*.log`, `.DS_Store`  
    - Prepend `**/` to a file or folder name (e.g. `**/.venv/`, `**/.DS_Store`) to also ignore it in subdirectories anywhere within the repository

---

## 📍 Common Problems

| Message or situation | What to do |
|----------------------|------------|
| `fatal: not a git repository` | You are not inside a repository folder. Use `pwd` and `cd` to find your project folder. |
| `Your branch is behind 'origin/main'` | Run `git pull`. |
| `rejected ... failed to push some refs` | The remote has commits you do not have. Run `git pull`, fix any conflicts, then `git push` again. |
| `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in <file>` | Open the file, resolve the `<<<<<<<` / `=======` / `>>>>>>>` sections, then `git add <file>` and `git commit`. |
| `nothing to commit, working tree clean` | Nothing has changed since the last commit. Nothing to do. |
| `git commit` opens a strange text editor (Vim) | You forgot `-m "message"`. In Vim, type `:q!` and press `Enter` to quit, then run the command again with `-m`. |
